13|DESCRIPTION
14|       man formats and displays the on-line manual pages.  If you specify sec-

16|       the  name of the manual page, which is typically the name of a command,
17|       function, or file.  However, if name contains  a  slash  (/)  then  man
18|       interprets  it  as a file specification, so that you can do man ./foo.5
19|       or even man /cd/foo/bar.1.gz.

22|       files.

00|
01|       If you don't specify -M but set the MANPATH environment  variable,  the
02|       value  of  that  variable  is  the  list  of  the  directories that man
03|       searches.
04|
05|       If you don't specify an explicit path list  with  -M  or  MANPATH,  man
06|       develops  its  own path list based on the contents of the configuration
07|       file /private/etc/man.conf.  The MANPATH statements in  the  configura-
08|       tion  file  identify  particular  directories  to include in the search
09|       path.
10|
11|       Furthermore, the MANPATH_MAP statements add to the search path  depend-
12|       ing  on your command search path (i.e. your PATH environment variable).
13|       For each directory that may be in  the  command  search  path,  a  MAN-
14|       PATH_MAP  statement  specifies  a directory that should be added to the
15|       search path for manual page files.  man looks at the PATH variable  and
16|       adds the corresponding directories to the manual page file search path.
17|       Thus, with the proper use of MANPATH_MAP, when you  issue  the  command
18|       man  xyz,  you  get a manual page for the program that would run if you
19|       issued the command xyz.
20|
21|       In addition, for each directory in the command search path (we'll  call
22|       it  a  "command  directory")  for  which  you do not have a MANPATH_MAP
23|       statement, man automatically looks for a manual page directory "nearby"
